title: Sinking funds: saving for the known unknowns
description: Some expenses are surprises; others are certainties wearing a disguise. Sinking funds are how you save for the second kind.

body.heading: Not if, but when
paragraphs: Cars need tyres. Phones crack. Friends get married in expensive cities. None of these are true emergencies — they are irregular certainties. A sinking fund is a pot you feed monthly for one specific future cost.
The idea is kitchen-table simple: if you know a cost is coming, start paying for it now, in small pieces, while it is still cheap to do so.

body.heading: One pot per purpose
paragraphs: Common sinking funds cover car repairs, gifts, holidays, annual bills, and replacing technology. If replacing a $600 phone in two years matters to you, that is $25 a month starting now — painless compared with finding $600 in a panic.
Keep the pots separate, or track them in a simple list if your bank allows only one savings account. What matters is that each pot has a name, a target, and a monthly amount.

body.heading: They change how surprises feel
paragraphs: The first time a "surprise" bill is paid calmly from its pot, the system proves itself. Sinking funds do not just organise money; they lower the background stress of knowing that life is expensive.
Start with just one fund — the expense that has ambushed you most recently. One working pot teaches the method better than five theoretical ones, and you can add the next fund at the next payday.

takeaway: For every cost you know is coming — repairs, gifts, replacements — start a small monthly pot now, and let future you be pleasantly unsurprised.
